vanuatu: Vanuatu is a Y-shaped archipelago of about 83 relatively small islands of volcanic origin, 65 of them inhabited, with about 1,300 kilometres between the most northern and southern islands. It lies 1,750 km east of northern Australia and 540 km northeast of New Caledonia. The largest island is Espiritu Santo, and the highest point is Mount Tabwemasana, at 1,879 metres. Most islands are steep, with unstable soils and little permanent freshwater. There are several active volcanoes, including Lopevi and Mount Yasur, and volcanic activity is common.

The history before European colonisation is mostly obscure, since no written sources predate contact and little archaeological work has been done. Evidence gathered since the 1980s supports the settlement of the islands about 3,000 years ago, between roughly 1100 BCE and 700 BCE, by people almost certainly of the Lapita culture. Notable Lapita sites include Teouma on Éfaté, which has a large ancient cemetery containing the remains of 94 individuals. Sites on Éfaté, Lelepa and Eretoka are associated with the 16th–17th century chief or chiefs called Roy Mata, a title possibly held by different men over several generations, who according to oral tradition united local clans and presided over an era of peace.

The first Europeans to visit were a Spanish expedition led by the Portuguese navigator Fernandes de Queirós, who reached Espíritu Santo in 1606 and claimed the archipelago for Spain as La Austrialia del Espíritu Santo. James Cook named it the New Hebrides in 1774, after the Hebrides of Scotland. In the 1880s France and the United Kingdom claimed parts of it, and in 1906 they agreed to manage it jointly as an Anglo-French condominium. An independence movement arose in the 1970s, and the Republic of Vanuatu was founded in 1980. The name combines vanua, meaning land or home, and tu, to stand; the first prime minister, Walter Lini, said it was meant to connote a country that has stood alone.

Vanuatu is a parliamentary democracy with a written constitution, and its capital is Port Vila on Efate. The official languages are Bislama, English and French, and Bislama, a creole with a mostly English-derived vocabulary, is the lingua franca. The Lapita sites became the country's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008. A national Council of Chiefs, the Malvatu Mauri, advises the government on culture and language, and chiefs remain leading figures at village level. The country is a member of the United Nations, the Commonwealth of Nations and the Pacific Islands Forum.
vatican-city: The territory of Vatican City covers 44 hectares and forms part of the Vatican Hill and the adjacent former Vatican Fields, on the west bank of the Tiber. Until 1929 the area belonged to the Roman rione of Borgo. It is enclosed largely by walls: those of Leo IV (847–855), later expanded by fortifications built under Paul III (1534–1549), Pius IV (1559–1565) and Urban VIII (1623–1644).

St Peter's Square is set apart from Italian territory only by a white line along its limit. Some properties of the Holy See elsewhere in Rome and Italy, notably the Papal Palace of Castel Gandolfo and the major basilicas, have extraterritorial status similar to that of foreign embassies.

In the Roman Republic the name Vatican applied to the Ager Vaticanus, a marshy area on the west bank of the Tiber. Its closeness to the Etruscan city of Veii, an old enemy of Rome, and the floods of the Tiber led the Romans to regard it as dismal and ominous. Agrippina the Elder drained the area and laid out gardens there in the early 1st century CE, and in 40 CE her son, the emperor Caligula, built a circus for charioteers, later completed by Nero.

The Vatican obelisk in St Peter's Square is the last visible remnant of that circus. Caligula brought it from Heliopolis in Roman Egypt. The circus became a site of martyrdom for many Christians after the Great Fire of Rome in 64, and tradition states that Saint Peter was crucified upside-down there. In 1586 Pope Sixtus V moved the obelisk to its present position, using a method devised by the architect Domenico Fontana. The name Vatican City was first used in the Lateran Treaty, signed on 11 February 1929.

Vatican City is an absolute elective monarchy in which the pope holds legislative, executive and judicial power. Legislative authority is exercised in his name by the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State, a body of cardinals appointed for five-year periods. The state is distinct from the Holy See, which has existed as a juridical entity since Roman Imperial times and was not interrupted when it lacked territory between 1870 and 1929.

Citizenship rests on appointment to work in the service of the Holy See, not on birth, and usually ends when the appointment does. In 2024 the population was 882 residents, and a further 372 citizens lived elsewhere. Legislation uses only Italian. The state earns income from stamps, coins, museum admissions and publications, and uses the euro. UNESCO listed Vatican City as a World Heritage Site in 1984, the only site that consists of an entire state.
verica: Verica's coinage presents him as a son of Commius and king of the Atrebates, a tribe that was probably Belgic. His predecessors are likely to have influenced a wide area covering Berkshire, Surrey, western Kent, Sussex, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. The distribution of his own coins shows a much smaller kingdom, limited to modern Sussex and east Hampshire, with its capital in or near the later Roman town of Noviomagus Reginorum, the modern Chichester. He succeeded his elder brother Eppillus in about 15 CE.

He may also have ruled the northern Atrebatic kingdom at Calleva Atrebatum, the modern Silchester. Rome recognised him as rex, and he appears to have had friendly trading and diplomatic links with the empire, perhaps in an attempt to restore the kingdom to its former strength. Unlike those of nearby areas, the hillforts in the core of his kingdom show no sign of refortification, which implies that its inhabitants were well disposed to Rome.

The Catuvellauni pressed on his territory from the east. Epaticcus, brother of Cunobelinus, conquered Calleva in about 25 CE. After the death of Epaticcus about 35 CE Verica regained some territory, but Caratacus, the son of Cunobelinus, conquered the entire kingdom some time after 40 CE. By the time of his expulsion the kingdom had been reduced to a core around Chichester and the Manhood Peninsula.

Dio Cassius records that a Berikos, widely taken to be Verica, fled to the emperor Claudius because of a revolt, and Suetonius mentions British demands that Rome return certain deserters. His ties with Rome have been used to argue that the invasion landed on the south coast and not at the traditional site of Richborough in Kent. He may have been restored afterwards, but this is not attested, and a new ruler of the region, Cogidubnus, soon appeared; he may have been Verica's heir.

Most scholars take Verica to have been a man. The archaeologist Miles Russell has argued that Verica was a woman, citing the ending of the name and the horsewomen on the coinage. Roger Tomlin disputes this, since no female client ruler is known to have used the title rex, and Daphne Nash notes that some coins show Verica with an Adam's apple and in male priestly dress.
victor-hugo: Victor-Marie Hugo was born on 26 February 1802 in Besançon, the youngest son of Joseph Léopold Sigisbert Hugo, a general in the Napoleonic army, and Sophie Trébuchet. His father was an atheist and an ardent supporter of the Republic, while his mother was loyal to the deposed dynasty. Because his father was an officer, the family moved often from posting to posting. In 1810 his father was made Count Hugo de Cogolludo y Sigüenza by Joseph Bonaparte, then King of Spain, though the Spanish title seems not to have been legally recognised in France.

In his youth Hugo resolved to be Chateaubriand or nothing, and his life came to parallel that of the older writer in many ways. Like him, he furthered the cause of Romanticism, became involved in politics and was forced into exile. He married Adèle Foucher in October 1822.

Hugo published his first novel, Hans of Iceland, in 1823 and his second, Bug-Jargal, in 1826. His five volumes of poetry between 1829 and 1840 cemented his reputation as one of the great elegiac and lyric poets of his time. The Hunchback of Notre-Dame appeared in 1831 and Les Misérables in 1862. He was at the forefront of Romanticism with his play Cromwell and his drama Hernani. After three unsuccessful attempts he was elected to the Académie française in 1841, and he wrote the libretto of Louise Bertin's opera La Esmeralda in 1836.

Politically he moved from royalism toward republicanism. Louis Philippe I appointed him a peer of France in 1845, where he spoke against the death penalty and social injustice and for freedom of the press. Elected in 1848 to the National Assembly of the Second Republic as a conservative, he broke with the conservatives in 1849 with a speech calling for an end to misery and poverty. His campaign to abolish the death penalty was known internationally.

When Louis Napoleon seized complete power in 1851, Hugo openly declared him a traitor to France. He moved to Brussels, then to Jersey, from which he was expelled for supporting the newspaper L'Homme. He settled at Hauteville House in Saint Peter Port, Guernsey, in self-imposed exile from October 1855 until 1870. He returned to Paris in 1870 and was hailed as a national hero. He lost a bid for re-election to the National Assembly in 1872 and was elected to the new Senate on 30 January 1876.

Hugo died on 22 May 1885, aged 83. He was given a state funeral in the Panthéon of Paris, attended by over two million people, the largest in French history. He produced more than 4,000 drawings, with about 3,000 surviving. His portrait was placed on French currency.
vienna: Vienna lies in north-eastern Austria at the easternmost extension of the Alps, on the eastern edge of the Vienna Woods and at the transition to the Pannonian Basin. The earliest settlement, on the site of the inner city, lay south of the meandering Danube, and the city now spans both banks. It is both a city and one of the nine states of Austria. The name is a Latinised form of the German Wien, which comes from the River Wien and first appears in the Salzburg Annals, recording a battle at a place called Wenia in 881.

In the 1st century the Romans set up the military camp of Vindobona, in the province of Pannonia, near the Danube to secure the frontier. Construction of the legionary camp began around 97 CE, and the settlement at its peak had about 15,000 people. The emperor Marcus Aurelius may have died here in 180. The city was rebuilt after a Germanic invasion and served as a seat of Roman government until the fifth century, when its people fled the Huns and the site was abandoned for several centuries.

In 1155 Vienna became the seat of the Babenbergs, who ruled Austria from 976 to 1246, and in 1221 it was granted city rights. In the 16th century the Habsburgs made it the seat of the emperors of the Holy Roman Empire, which it remained until the empire's dissolution in 1806, with only a brief interruption. With the formation of the Austrian Empire in 1804 it became the capital of that empire and of all its successor states.

As capital of Austria-Hungary from 1867 to 1918 it grew sharply, and in 1910 it had more than two million inhabitants and was the third-largest city in Europe after London and Paris. Under the Nazi regime 65,000 Jews were deported from Vienna and murdered, and about 130,000 fled.

Vienna is the capital and most populous city of Austria, with just over two million inhabitants. The historic centre was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001 and includes Baroque palaces and gardens and the Ringstrasse of the late 19th century. Beethoven, Haydn, Mozart, Schubert and Brahms were among the composers who worked there, and Sigmund Freud, the first psychoanalyst, lived there too. Since 1980 the city has been a United Nations headquarters city.
vietnam: Vietnam lies on the eastern Indochinese Peninsula, with a total area of about 331,000 square kilometres, a coastline 3,444 kilometres long and land boundaries of 4,639 kilometres. At its narrowest point, in Quảng Trị province, it is as little as 50 kilometres across, and in the north it widens to around 600 kilometres.

The land is mostly hilly and densely forested, with level land covering no more than 20%. The Red River flows past Hanoi into the Gulf of Tonkin, and its delta, a plain of 15,000 square kilometres, has the highest population density of any region; its sediment advances the delta 60 to 80 metres into the South China Sea every year.

Humans lived in what is now Vietnam as early as the Paleolithic, and Homo erectus fossils dating to around 500,000 BCE have been found in caves in the north. By about 1,000 BCE wet-rice cultivation in the Ma River and Red River floodplains led to the Đông Sơn culture, known for its bronze casting and elaborate bronze drums.

Vietnamese legends hold that the Hồng Bàng dynasty of the Hùng kings, first established in 2879 BCE, was the first state, known as Văn Lang. In 257 BCE the last Hùng king was defeated by Thục Phán, who formed Âu Lạc and proclaimed himself An Dương Vương. The Han dynasty annexed northern and central Vietnam, which were then under Chinese rule from 111 BCE until the first dynasty emerged in 939.

Successive monarchical dynasties absorbed Chinese influences through Confucianism and Buddhism and expanded southward to the Mekong Delta, conquering Champa. During most of the 17th and 18th centuries Vietnam was effectively divided into two domains, Đàng Trong and Đàng Ngoài. The Nguyễn, the last imperial dynasty, surrendered to France in 1883, and in 1887 the territory was integrated into French Indochina as three separate regions. The Viet Minh launched the August Revolution and declared independence in 1945. France returned and was defeated in the First Indochina War in 1954, after which Vietnam was divided into two parts.

The Vietnam War was fought between communist North Vietnam, supported by the Soviet Union and China, and anti-communist South Vietnam, supported by the United States. After the North Vietnamese victory in 1975 the country reunified as a communist state under the Communist Party of Vietnam. An ineffective planned economy, a Western trade embargo and wars with Cambodia and China crippled it further, and in 1986 the party launched the Đổi Mới reforms toward a socialist-oriented market economy. Vietnam joined the World Trade Organization in 2007. Its population was 96,208,984 in the 2019 census; the Kinh make up 85.32% of it, and 54 ethnic groups are officially recognised.
vikramaditya-i: Vikramaditya was one of several sons of Pulakeshin II; the later Chalukyas of Kalyani made him a son of Pulakeshin's son Adityavarman, a statement that can be dismissed as inaccurate. Pulakeshin was defeated and probably killed when the Pallavas invaded Vatapi around 642, and the history of the next decade is unclear. The throne may have passed to Adityavarman, his son Abhinavaditya and then another brother, Chandraditya, whose widow Vijaya-Bhattarika appears to have acted as regent for their minor son.

During that regency Vikramaditya seems to have risen as supreme commander of the army and ruler in practice. His inscriptions say that he recovered the regal fortune of his father, which had been concealed by three kings. The historian K. A. Nilakanta Sastri took these to include his brothers and supposed a partition of the kingdom, but there is no evidence of one; D. C. Sircar and others hold that he fought the Pallavas as a subordinate of his brothers and took the throne only after their deaths. His Gadval inscription of about 674, dated to his twelfth regnal year, places his accession about 655.

With the help of his maternal grandfather, a king of the Western Ganga dynasty, Vikramaditya ended a Pallava occupation that had lasted thirteen years. He gave his loyal younger brother Jayasimhavarma the viceroyalty of Lata in southern Gujarat. Against the Pallava kings Mahendravarman II and Paramesvaravarman I he allied himself with the Pandyas, and by 670 he had a military camp at Malliyur, west of Kanchipuram. Chalukya records claim that he defeated Paramesvaravarman I and took Kanchi but did not destroy it; the writer Anirudh Kanisetti holds that the city was sacked.

Chalukya records place him in camp at Uragapura on the south bank of the Kaveri river on 25 April 674. At Peruvalanallur he met Paramesvaravarman I and a Pandya king, and Pallava and Pandya records alike claim that the Chalukyas were defeated there. Pallava inscriptions also speak of the destruction of the city of Ranarasika, an epithet of Vikramaditya, but several historians question whether Vatapi was sacked a second time; Chalukya records credit his son Vinayaditya and grandson Vijayaditya with defeating the invaders.

Vikramaditya bore titles that advertised his military power, among them Rana-rasika, lover of war, Anivarita, unopposed, and Raja-malla, royal wrestler. He was married to the Western Ganga princess Gangamahadevi. Under him the Chalukya kingdom recovered most of the territory it had controlled under Pulakeshin II. He died in 680 and was succeeded by his son Vinayaditya.
vincent-van-gogh: Vincent Willem van Gogh was born on 30 March 1853 in Groot-Zundert, in the predominantly Catholic province of North Brabant. He was the oldest surviving child of Theodorus van Gogh, a minister of the Dutch Reformed Church, and Anna Cornelia Carbentus. His grandfather, also named Vincent, was a prominent art dealer, and three of that grandfather's six sons became art dealers. His younger brother Theo was born on 1 May 1857. Van Gogh was taught at home, then sent to boarding school at Zevenbergen and in 1866 to the middle school in Tilburg, where he was deeply unhappy. He returned home in March 1868 and later wrote that his youth was "austere and cold, and sterile."

As an adult he began painting at an elementary level. In early 1882 his uncle Cornelis Marinus, owner of a gallery in Amsterdam, commissioned drawings of The Hague but was twice disappointed. Theo gave him money for materials in August 1882. From early 1883 Van Gogh worked on multi-figure compositions, and he destroyed several large paintings made at Nuenen; The Potato Eaters and its companion pieces are the only ones to survive. In November 1885 he travelled to Antwerp and later to Paris, where he met Émile Bernard and Paul Gauguin. His colours grew brighter, and his style was fully realised during his stay in Arles in 1888, when he painted series of olive trees, wheat fields and sunflowers.

The correspondence with Theo is the most comprehensive primary source on his work. It includes more than 600 letters from Vincent to Theo, and most of what is known of his theories of art is recorded in them.

Van Gogh suffered from psychotic episodes and delusions. His friendship with Gauguin ended after a confrontation with a razor, when he severed part of his own left ear. He spent time in psychiatric hospitals, including one at Saint-Rémy, and then moved to the Auberge Ravoux in Auvers-sur-Oise, where he came under the care of Dr Paul Gachet. On 27 July 1890 he shot himself in the chest and died two days later.

His reputation grew steadily among artists and critics after exhibitions in the late 1880s. Theo died in January 1891, and Theo's widow Jo van Gogh-Bonger took charge of the paintings and letters. Memorial exhibitions were held in several cities, and in 1896 the young Henri Matisse was introduced to Van Gogh's work and turned to bright colours. The Fauves and German Expressionists later took up elements of his style.
virgil: Biographical information about Virgil comes chiefly from ancient vitae, or lives, prefixed to commentaries on his work by Probus, Donatus and Servius. The life given by Donatus is thought to reproduce closely a lost life by Suetonius. Some of this evidence relies on allegory and on inferences drawn from his poetry, so details of his life are considered somewhat problematic.

According to the vitae, Publius Vergilius Maro was born on 15 October 70 BCE in the village of Andes, near Mantua in Cisalpine Gaul, in what is now northern Italy. His ancestry is uncertain, and scholars have proposed Etruscan, Celtic, Venetic, Ligurian or Greek origins. Most sources say his father was an employee of an apparitor named Magius, whose daughter he married. Phocas and Probus give his mother's name as Magia Polla. Confusion between the family name Magius and the noun magus, 'magician', probably contributed to the medieval legend that Virgil was a magician.

The commentators say Virgil began school at five and later went to Cremona, Milan and finally Rome to study rhetoric, medicine and astronomy, which he abandoned for philosophy. His admiring references to Asinius Pollio and Cinna have led scholars to infer that he was for a time associated with the neoteric circle of Catullus. According to the Catalepton, he began to write poetry while in the Epicurean school of Siro in Naples. A group of small works attributed to him by the commentators, the Appendix Vergiliana, is considered spurious by modern scholars, with the possible exception of some short pieces.

The Eclogues are ten poems in dactylic hexameter, roughly modelled on the pastoral poetry of the Hellenistic poet Theocritus. Eclogues 1 and 9 address the land confiscations and their effects on the Italian countryside. Eclogue 4, addressed to Asinius Pollio and called the Messianic Eclogue, uses the imagery of a golden age in connection with the birth of a child whose identity has been debated. Virgil is credited with establishing Arcadia as a poetic ideal. Modern scholars largely reject attempts to draw his biography from the characters of the poems.

His works revolutionised Latin poetry almost from publication, and the Eclogues, Georgics and above all the Aeneid became standard school texts. Ovid parodied the opening of the Aeneid, Lucan wrote an anti-Virgilian epic, and Statius and Silius Italicus engaged closely with him. Servius, a commentator of the 4th century CE, based his work on that of Donatus. Augustine of Hippo confessed that he had wept at reading the death of Dido. In the Divine Comedy Dante presents Virgil as his guide through Hell and most of Purgatory.
vladimir-lenin: Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov was born in Simbirsk on 22 April 1870 (10 April O.S.), the third of eight children. His father, Ilya Nikolayevich Ulyanov, came from a family of former serfs and rose to be Director of Public Schools for the province, a post that carried hereditary nobility. Lenin took up revolutionary socialist politics after his brother's execution in 1887 and was expelled from Kazan Imperial University for protesting against the Tsarist government. In late 1893 he moved to Saint Petersburg and rose to a senior position in a Marxist cell. Arrested for sedition in 1897, he argued in prison that industrial capitalism had created a proletariat that would overthrow Tsarism. He was exiled to Siberia, where he married Nadezhda Krupskaya.

In 1903 Lenin took a key part in the split of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party and led the Bolshevik faction. After the failed Revolution of 1905 he campaigned for the First World War to be turned into a Europe-wide proletarian revolution. He returned to Russia after the February Revolution of 1917 and helped lead the October Revolution, in which the Bolsheviks overthrew the Provisional Government.

His government at first shared power with the Left Socialist Revolutionaries. The Constituent Assembly elected in November 1917 gave the Bolsheviks about a quarter of the vote; it met in January 1918 and was forcibly disbanded. By 1919 Mensheviks and Socialist Revolutionaries had been expelled from the soviets and Russia was a one-party state. The government redistributed land, nationalised banks and large industry, left the First World War by a treaty conceding territory, and won the Russian Civil War. Opponents were suppressed in the Red Terror, in which tens of thousands were killed or interned. In 1921 Lenin encouraged economic growth through the New Economic Policy.

Lenin fell seriously ill in 1921, suffered strokes in May and December 1922, and died at Gorki on 21 January 1924. Joseph Stalin succeeded him as the pre-eminent figure in the Soviet government. His interpretation of Marxism, first called Leninism by Martov in 1904, became the basis of Marxism-Leninism and a model for later Communist-led states. Supporters see him as a champion of revolutionary socialism and internationalism, while critics accuse him of establishing a totalitarian dictatorship that carried out mass killings and political repression.
voltaire: François-Marie Arouet, later known as Voltaire, was born in Paris, the youngest of five children of François Arouet, a lawyer and minor treasury official, and Marie Marguerite Daumard, whose family was of the lowest rank of the French nobility. He gave his birth date as 20 February 1694, claiming to be the illegitimate son of a nobleman, but his birth is dated to 21 November 1694, with a baptism on 22 November. The Jesuits educated him at the Collège Louis-le-Grand from 1704 to 1711, where he was taught Latin, theology and rhetoric.

Voltaire's play Artémire flopped in 1720, and he turned to an epic poem about Henry IV of France, La Henriade. Denied a licence to publish it, he went north in August 1722 to find a publisher outside France, and in the Netherlands he was impressed by the openness and tolerance of Dutch society. The poem was printed clandestinely in Rouen, and when copies were smuggled into Paris it was an instant success. His play Mariamne failed in 1724 but did better in a reworked version in April 1725.

In early 1726 Guy Auguste de Rohan-Chabot had Voltaire beaten by servants after a quarrel about his name change. When Voltaire challenged him to a duel, the powerful Rohan family had him imprisoned without trial in the Bastille on 17 April 1726. Fearing indefinite imprisonment, he asked to be exiled to England instead, and on 2 May he was escorted from the Bastille to Calais and embarked.

He was one of the first authors to be commercially successful internationally, and wrote more than 20,000 letters and 2,000 books and pamphlets. In February 1778 he returned to Paris for the first time in over 25 years, partly for the opening of his tragedy Irène, and died there on 30 May 1778. The Church had refused him a Christian burial because he would not retract his criticism, so friends buried him secretly at the Abbey of Scellières.

Voltaire produced plays, poems, novels, essays, histories and scientific expositions. His best-known work is the novella Candide (1759), which ridicules Gottfried Leibniz's belief that this is the best of all possible worlds. His History of Charles XII (1731), The Age of Louis XIV (1751) and Essay on the Customs and the Spirit of the Nations (1756) set aside diplomatic and military narrative for customs, social history and the arts and sciences, and treated Europe as a whole.
